1128.title: The hand that points to the foot
1128.hook: one arm swings across the body like an elephant's trunk and points at a lifted foot: why Hindus bow at the feet

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: samhara, the ending is God's work too, the flame held level with the drum. Today, the lower hands, and where one of them points.

segments.voice: A guide at a busy train station doesn't take your suitcase or drag you to the platform. She lifts an arm and points: that way. Then she lets you walk. Nataraja has a hand like that. Of his two lower hands, one is raised palm out, the do-not-fear gesture from the mudras. The other is the one to watch today. It swings across his chest and hangs loose, and the fingers point down and across the body, at his raised foot.
screen: `A GUIDE WHO POINTS: THAT WAY.` → `ONE LOWER HAND: DO NOT FEAR.` → `THE OTHER POINTS AT THE FOOT.`

segments.voice: That arm has a name in the language of dance: gaja hasta, the elephant hand, because it hangs across the body the way an elephant's trunk swings. Notice what the hand doesn't do. It doesn't hold anything, or grab, or push. It points, at the lifted foot. One foot is planted, pressing down; what's under it comes tomorrow. The other foot is lifted clear of the ground. In the usual reading, the planted foot presses down and holds, and the lifted foot is grace: release, the way out. Here is grace, says the hand. Look there. And that's the teaching behind a gesture you'll see in any Hindu family. The feet of the divine are where grace is, so they're where you bow. In temples, flowers are laid at the god's feet. In devotional poetry, taking refuge at the Lord's feet means surrender, trust, coming home. And because parents, elders and teachers are honored as people that blessing flows through, children bend and touch their feet, and get a hand on the head in return. The Tamil poet-saint Appar sang of this foot. In paraphrase: if you could see the arched brow, the smile, the matted hair and the lifted golden foot of the dancer, being born a human would be worth it. So when a kid touches a grandmother's feet before an exam, that's the pointing hand, at home: grace is there; bow there. The hand doesn't drag you. It points, and leaves the walking to you.
screen: `GAJA HASTA, THE ELEPHANT HAND.` · `IT DOESN'T GRAB. IT POINTS.` · `THE LIFTED FOOT: GRACE, RELEASE.` · `WHY HINDUS BOW AT THE FEET.` · `APPAR: WORTH BEING BORN FOR.` · then, large: `GRACE IS THERE. BOW THERE.`

segments.voice: If an elder is near you today, a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, you might bend and touch their feet, or bow to them in your heart. Then rest your left arm loosely across your lap, fingers pointing down, and follow its line to your feet. Feel one foot planted, let the other feel light, and breathe there. If you pray, bring your thoughts to the feet of Shiva, or of God.

1129.title: Held down, never killed
1129.hook: under the planted foot lies a small figure, ignorance itself, and the dancer never finishes him off

segments.voice: Yesterday: his lifted foot is grace; refuge is at his feet. That's where the elephant hand points, and where Hindus bow. Today, the other foot, and who's under it.

segments.voice: He's the easiest part of the image to miss. Look down past the swinging arms and the flying hair to Nataraja's right foot, the planted one. Under it, flat on his belly, lies a small, round-limbed figure, often holding a snake, pinned to the ground. He isn't the hero of anything. He's closer to the name that was right there a second ago, or the reason you walked into this room: gone. Small, daily, and always back. His name is Apasmara.
screen: `EASY TO MISS.` → `UNDER THE PLANTED FOOT.` → `HIS NAME: APASMARA.`

segments.voice: In the usual reading, Apasmara is ignorance: the forgetting that hides what's true. Hindu teachers have a word for it, avidya, not-knowing, and in much of Hindu thought it's the root trouble, deeper than any enemy outside you: forgetting who you really are, and forgetting God. There's a story behind him, told in the temple tradition of Chidambaram and retold by the art historian Ananda Coomaraswamy. In a forest lived a community of sages, proud of their own rites, who thought they had no need of Shiva. He came among them in disguise, and they were furious, so they used their powers against him. First they sent a tiger. Shiva caught it, peeled off its skin, and wore it at his waist. Then a snake: he hung it around his neck like a garland. Then a dwarf, a malicious little creature. Shiva put his foot on its back and began to dance, and the sages, watching, gave up their pride. Here's the detail worth keeping. Shiva never kills Apasmara. He keeps him under the foot, and keeps dancing. Many teachers read that as honest: ignorance doesn't vanish for good in one blow. It's held down, again and again, by remembering. That's why so much Hindu practice is repetition: a name said on every bead of a mala, a lamp lit every evening, the same prayer before every meal. Each one is the foot pressing down again. Remembering isn't a victory you win once. It's a step you keep taking.
screen: `APASMARA: IGNORANCE, AVIDYA.` · `TIGER, SNAKE, DWARF FROM THE SAGES.` · `HE IS HELD DOWN, NEVER KILLED.` · `WHY HINDU PRACTICE REPEATS.` · then, large: `REMEMBERING IS A STEP YOU KEEP TAKING.`

segments.voice: With both feet flat on the floor, rest your attention in the right foot: the heel, the ball, the toes. When the mind wanders off into a plan or a memory, that's Apasmara, and it's fine: press the right foot gently into the floor and come back. If you pray, say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, each time you come back, the way a mala is told bead by bead; if not, just say here.

1130.title: The river in Shiva's hair
1130.hook: a river caught in the dancer's hair: why the Ganga is holy, and why water is poured on Shiva
1130.carry: ganga came down through shiva to free souls

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the real enemy is ignorance, held down by remembering. Apasmara stays under the foot, never killed. Today, the hair, and who's caught in it.
screen: `IGNORANCE, HELD DOWN BY REMEMBERING.` · `TODAY: WHO'S CAUGHT IN THE HAIR.`

segments.voice: Get close to a Nataraja bronze and look at the hair. It doesn't hang down. It flies out to both sides in long locks, like the spokes of a wheel, as if he's spinning so fast the hair can't keep up. And tangled in them on one side is something tiny: a little woman, half of her shaped like flowing water, her hands folded. That's the river Ganga.
screen: `THE HAIR FLIES OUT LIKE SPOKES.` → `AS IF HE'S SPINNING.` → `CAUGHT IN THE LOCKS: GANGA.`

segments.voice: Why is a river in his hair? The Ramayana tells it. Long ago, the sixty thousand sons of King Sagara were burned to ash by the anger of a sage, Kapila, and their souls had no rest. Only the heavenly Ganga, flowing over their ashes, could free them. Two generations tried to bring her down, and failed. Then Bhagiratha practiced austerities so long and so hard that the gods agreed. But a river falling from heaven would break the earth. So Bhagiratha turned to Shiva, and Shiva stood beneath the falling river and took her on his head. She vanished into his matted locks, gentled, until he let her out in streams. Bhagiratha led her across the land to the ashes, and his ancestors were set free. That's why the Ganga is the holiest river in Hindu life. Families carry the ashes of their dead to her, hoping for the same release. Homes keep a small sealed pot of Ganga water for prayers, and for the dying. And in Shiva temples, water is poured over the linga again and again; many devotees say it recalls this moment, the river landing on his head. Even the word stuck: in many Indian languages, a huge, patient effort is still called a Bhagiratha effort. So when a family in New Jersey flies an urn to Haridwar, or a grandmother keeps that little pot on her shelf, they're stepping into Bhagiratha's story: doing the long work for those who came before. And the wildest part of the dancer, his flying hair, is holding that river with care.
screen: `SAGARA'S SONS: ASHES WITHOUT REST.` · `BHAGIRATHA BRINGS DOWN THE GANGA.` · `SHIVA CATCHES HER IN HIS HAIR.` · `WHY ASHES GO TO THE GANGA.` · `WHY WATER IS POURED ON SHIVA.` · then, large: `SHE CAME DOWN TO SET SOULS FREE.`

segments.voice: If you can, fill a small cup of water. Pour it slowly, in a thin stream, the way water is poured over Shiva in a temple: over a plant, or into your other palm. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya with the stream, or offer it to God in your own words. If you don't, think of someone who came before you, and of the long effort it took to get you here. segments.voice: At Chidambaram, in Tamil Nadu, the dancing Shiva isn't in a museum case. He stands in a hall with a golden roof, dressed, garlanded, bathed and sung to, while a crowd presses forward and oil lamps are waved in the dark. Temple tradition says this is where he danced for two sages who longed to see it: Patanjali, shown with the body of a serpent, and Vyaghrapada, whose name means tiger-foot. And beside the dancer hangs a curtain. At certain moments a priest draws it back, and the people lean in.
screen: `A HALL WITH A GOLDEN ROOF.` → `THE DANCE FOR TWO SAGES.` → `A CURTAIN BESIDE THE DANCER.`

segments.voice: Behind the curtain there seems to be nothing: an empty space, hung with a garland of golden bilva leaves. It's called the Chidambara rahasya, the secret of Chidambaram. The dancer is there in form, with arms and hair and fire. And right beside him, the same lord, with no form at all. Space. Tradition links this temple with space itself, the open sky the dance happens in. Now put the whole image back together, because a Shaiva teaching does exactly that. It reads the dance as doing five things at once. The drum: creation. The raised hand that says do not fear: preservation, keeping what's made. The flame: dissolution. The planted foot on Apasmara: concealment, the veil of forgetting that hides what's true. And the lifted foot the elephant hand points to: grace, release. Make, keep, end, hide, free: five acts, one dancer, never stopping. And then the curtain opens on the space beside him. This is a teaching Hindus live with every day: God with form and God beyond form are not two gods. So a grandmother can bathe and dress an image with real tenderness, and say in the same breath that God is everywhere and no image holds him. The secret isn't locked away. It's shown, on purpose, to anyone standing in the crowd. The tradition doesn't ask anyone to choose between the dancer and the empty space. It keeps them side by side, behind one curtain.
screen: `THE SECRET: AN EMPTY SPACE.` · `FIVE ACTS: MAKE, KEEP, END, HIDE, FREE.` · `WITH FORM, AND BEYOND FORM.` · `NOT TWO GODS.` · then, large: `THE SAME LORD, WITH FORM AND AS SPACE.`

segments.voice: If there's an image of God near you, a picture, a statue, a lamp, look at it for a few breaths with care, the way a devotee looks at the dancer. Then close your eyes and notice the space around you, the quiet behind the sounds, and rest there, holding the image and the space together without choosing. If you pray, say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, into that space; if not, just rest in it.

segments.voice: A woman is Mom to her kids, Auntie to her nephew, a last name to her boss, and a nickname to her oldest friend. One person, and every name catches her from a different side. Hindu tradition does this with the divine, on purpose, and at length. Some hymns are nothing but names, one after another, like beads on a string. Today i'll open one of them: the Shiva Sahasranama.
screen: `ONE PERSON, MANY NAMES.` → `A HYMN MADE OF NAMES.` → `THE SHIVA SAHASRANAMA.`

segments.voice: Sahasranama is the hymn's own name for itself: the thousand names. Shiva has more than one such hymn; this one is in the Mahabharata, and it comes with a story. Krishna wants a son, so he climbs to the Himalayan hermitage of an old sage, Upamanyu. And Upamanyu tells him how he found Shiva. As a poor boy in the forest he once tasted milk, and came home begging for more. His mother had none. She stirred flour into water and gave him that, and when he knew the difference, she told him the truth: only Shiva could give him what he longed for. The boy turned to Shiva with his whole life, and in the epic's telling, Shiva came. Now, old, he hands Krishna the gift that costs nothing: the names. Near the start: Sthira, the firm one. Sthanu, the post. Prabhu, the lord. Bhima, the fearsome one. Sthanu is a plain word, a tree stump that doesn't move in the wind, and it sits right beside the dancer who never stops. The names don't argue. They stack. This is a Hindu teaching as old as the Rig Veda: truth is one, and the wise call it by many names. No single name says everything; each one is a door. So at a temple archana, a priest offers a flower at each name, a slow walk through the doors. And at home, the same Shiva might simply be Bholenath, the simple-hearted lord. One god, many names, and a devotee is allowed a favorite.
screen: `SAHASRANAMA: THE THOUSAND NAMES.` · `UPAMANYU: THE BOY WHO WANTED MILK.` · `STHANU: THE STEADY POST.` · `TRUTH IS ONE, CALLED BY MANY NAMES.` · then, large: `EACH NAME A DOOR.`

segments.voice: Choose three names of God you know, from any of these days, or the one your family uses. Say each one slowly, and after each, pause, as if you'd laid a flower down, the way an archana goes. If you pray, let each name be a small offering to Shiva, or to God. If you don't, say three words for what you most need: steady, kind, free, and pause after each.
The Shiva Sahasranama. A hymn of Shiva's names, said one at a time, each name a door into the one lord. Today's name from it: Sthanu, the steady post.

1133.howItsDone: Devotees greet Shiva with names like Shambho, Shankara and Nilakantha in songs and chants; the Shri Rudram, with its line namah shivaya, is chanted in Shiva temples, especially during abhisheka, and Om Namah Shivaya is repeated as a mantra.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shiva Sahasranama opened: one god, many names, and Sthanu, the steady post. Today, a fierce god's gentle names.
screen: `ONE GOD, MANY NAMES.` · `TODAY: TWO GENTLE NAMES.`

segments.voice: What do you call someone who frightens people and is still the one they run to? Shiva sits in cremation grounds, smeared with ash, a snake around his neck. Yesterday's list held Bhima, the fearsome one. And yet, in the bhajans sung at temples and in living rooms, the names you'll hear most are soft ones. Shambho. Shankara. Two names from the same hymn, and they don't sound frightening at all.
screen: `FEARSOME, AND STILL RUN TO.` → `SHAMBHO. SHANKARA.` → `THE GENTLE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Start with a story told to Hindu children everywhere. The gods and the demons churned the ocean of milk for the nectar of immortality. But before any treasure came up, out rose a poison so deadly it began to burn the worlds. Everyone ran. Everyone except Shiva, the wild one from the cremation grounds. He took the poison and drank it. In many tellings Parvati caught his throat so it wouldn't go down, and it stayed there and turned his throat blue. That's why one of his names is Nilakantha, the blue-throated. The fearsome one was the only one who could hold the harm. Now hear two of his names. Shankara: tradition explains it as the one who makes well-being, from sham, ease, and kara, the maker. Shambhu: the one from whom well-being comes. A Vedic hymn still chanted in temples, the Shri Rudram, keeps the same pattern. It opens by bowing to Rudra's anger and his arrows, not pretending he's harmless. Deep in the hymn it turns, and bows to him as Shambhu, as Shankara, as Shiva, the auspicious one. That's where the words namah shivaya are heard. So when the sahasranama puts Bhima, the fearsome, beside Shankara, it isn't confused. This is the teaching: in Hindu devotion, Shiva's fierceness is for well-being. He burns what harms and swallows what would poison. So when a family in a hospital waiting room quietly chants to Shiva, they aren't asking a frightening god to stay away. They're calling Shankara, the one who drank the poison so others wouldn't have to.
screen: `THE CHURNING OF THE OCEAN.` · `SHIVA DRINKS THE POISON: NILAKANTHA.` · `SHANKARA: THE MAKER OF WELL-BEING.` · `THE RUDRAM: FROM ANGER TO NAMAH SHIVAYA.` · then, large: `HIS FIERCENESS IS FOR WELL-BEING.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and breathe out slowly. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya on each out-breath, the words heard in the Rudram, five or eleven times, picturing the blue throat that held the world's poison. If you don't, bring to mind one fierce person in your life, and on each out-breath, name one thing their fierceness has protected.
The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's names from it: Shankara, the one who makes well-being, and Shambhu, from whom well-being comes. And the story behind them: Nilakantha, the blue-throated one.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shiva's fierceness is for our well-being. Shankara, Shambhu, and the blue throat. Today, the lord of creatures.
screen: `HIS FIERCENESS IS FOR WELL-BEING.` · `TODAY: THE LORD OF CREATURES.`

segments.voice: Kathmandu, early morning, beside the Bagmati river. Monkeys run along the temple walls. Pilgrims queue with marigolds, and a little way down the bank, smoke rises from the cremation ghats. The temple is Pashupatinath, and the name over its door is one of Shiva's: Pashupati. The animals in the courtyard are a fitting welcome, because the name is about them, and then about everyone.
screen: `A TEMPLE ON THE BAGMATI.` → `MONKEYS, MARIGOLDS, PILGRIMS.` → `PASHUPATI.`

segments.voice: Pashupati joins two words. Pati is lord. Pashu is a creature, the kind tied up in a yard: a cow, a goat. So at its simplest, Pashupati is the lord of animals, who looks after every living thing. A legend told in Nepal goes further. Shiva once left his mountain for the forest by the Bagmati, and there he roamed as a deer among the animals. The gods searched until they found him and caught him by the horn. The horn broke, and the piece left behind came to be worshipped where the temple stands. The lord of creatures had been one of them. Shaiva teachers then turned the name into a whole teaching, in schools such as Shaiva Siddhanta. Pati, the lord, is Shiva. Pashu is every soul, you and me included, called a creature because it's tied. And pasha is the rope. Teachers name its strands: a root ignorance that makes the soul feel small, the pull of past actions, and the hold of the changing world. And here is the Shaiva heart of it: the creature can't simply cut its own rope. The soul does its practice, and the lord loosens the rope, by grace. Humbling, because it puts everyone in the yard with the goats. Hopeful, because a rope can be untied, and someone is untying it. So when an old anger or a habit holds you like a tether, a Shaiva devotee doesn't just grit their teeth. They keep up the practice, and they ask Pashupati to loosen what they can't.
screen: `PASHU, PATI: CREATURE, LORD.` · `THE LORD WHO ROAMED AS A DEER.` · `PATI, PASHU, PASHA: LORD, SOUL, ROPE.` · `THE LORD LOOSENS IT, BY GRACE.` · then, large: `A ROPE CAN BE UNTIED.`

segments.voice: Ask quietly what's pulling at you today, a worry, a habit, a grudge, and feel where it tugs: the chest, the belly, the hands. If you pray, offer it the way names are offered in a temple: say Om Pashupataye Namah, I bow to the lord of creatures, slowly, eleven times, and on each one hand the knot to Shiva to loosen. If you'd like, set a flower or a little water before an image of him. If you don't pray, on each out-breath let the rope go a little slack, the way you'd loosen a knot without cutting it.
The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's name from it: Pashupati, lord of every creature, and in Shaiva teaching, the lord who loosens the soul's rope by grace.
